+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan pinched the edge of his stiff synth-silk collar, tugging it away from his throat for the fifth time in ten minutes. To a man who had spent twenty years in a pressurized canvas work-suit smelling of lubricant, ozone, and fine Martian regolith, formal terrestrial dress felt less like high fashion and more like a claustrophobic instrument of torture. The transfer vessel *Cydonia Express* hummed with the smooth, low vibration of nuclear-thermal maneuvering thrusters. Through the heavy quartz viewport, the rust-red disk of Mars was shrinking, replaced by the obsidian emptiness of high orbit and the glowing grid lines of distant orbital docks. Arthur wasn't alone in the lounge. Two men stood near the hydraulic airlock bulkhead, immaculately poised in crisp navy tunics emblazoned with a stylized red star over a gold olive branch. *The Antares Diplomatic Corps.* Arthur knew enough about off-world politics to recognize the contradiction inherent in that emblem. Antares, a thriving interstellar coalition three hundred light-years out, maintained a fleet of heavy battle-cruisers anchored just beyond the Sol System's jurisdictional boundary. Their diplomacy was backed by raw kinetic tonnage. When six of their sidearm-bearing guards had arrived at his remote moisture-and-mining station three hours ago, their request for an audience had carried the absolute authority of a military command. Arthur had possessed just enough self-preservation to recognize an imperative disguised as etiquette. A chime sounded—a clear, bell-like tone that echoed off the retro-futuristic brass trim and vacuum-sealed wall panels. Phosphor-green telemetry monitors overhead flickered as the ship matched velocity with an unseen station. "He will see you now, Mr. Neegan," one of the guards said, gesturing with a gloved hand toward the private stateroom door. Arthur swallowed, smoothed down his dark jacket, and stepped into the suite. The room was an extravagant display of off-world wealth. Teakwood paneling—real wood, imported across light-years at astronomical expense—lined the bulkheads, framing a wide, curved viewscreen. Seated behind a heavy desk of polished steel sat a man with silver-streaked hair, wearing a high-collared tunic that made Arthur’s own attire look like a beggar's rags. "Ah, Mr. Neegan. Please, sit." The man gestured to a leather-upholstered armchair. "I am Director Elijah Vane. Antares Special Ministry for Resource Allocation." Arthur sat down carefully, his heavy work boots clicking against the polished deck. "Director. I’d ask why I was pulled off my homestead by armed men, but I suspect it has something to do with the ninety thousand metric tons of Azra sitting beneath my dust-farm." Vane smiled—a thin, practiced expression that didn't reach his sharp gray eyes. He poured two measures of an amber liquid from a glass decanter, sliding one across the desk. "You are a pragmatic man, Arthur. That is refreshing. A simple first-generation mining engineer from the Cydonia sector who suddenly finds himself sitting atop the most valuable geological deposit in the known galaxy." "It's just rock to me," Arthur lied mildly, taking a cautious sip. The liquor was rich, smoky, and dangerously smooth. "Exotic rock, granted. But rock." "Do not play the ignorant colonist with me, Mr. Neegan. You hold a master's degree in applied isotopic geology from the Geneva Institute. You know precisely what Azra is." Vane leaned forward, resting his forearms on the steel desk. "It is not merely an exotic element. It is the catalyst that will dictate the next two centuries of human civilization." "It accelerates radioactive decay," Arthur said, falling back on the comfortable, objective neutrality of science. "Under a controlled magnetic field, Azra forces heavy radioactive isotopes to shed their energy in seconds rather than millennia, without triggering a critical prompt-neutron explosion. It turns inefficient sub-light engines into interstellar drives. It's a miracle for deep-space transport." "And weapons?" Vane asked softly. Arthur paused, his glass halfway to his mouth. "And weapons. A micro-gram of refined Azra introduced to a cobalt warhead would turn a tactical strike into a total planetary sterilization event. No defense grid in Sol could intercept the decay cascade in time." "Precisely," Vane said, his voice dropping an octave. "Which brings us to the political reality, Arthur. You hold the mineral title. The Martian Colonial Charter—drafted eighty years ago when Mars was considered an unprofitable dust heap—guarantees homesteaders total ownership of subsurface discoveries." "A clause the Earth-based mining corporations are currently trying to bribe the High Council to repeal," Arthur noted. "They won't get the chance," Vane countered smoothly. "Trans-Martian Ore has already dispatched a fleet of legal counsel—and four squads of corporate mercenaries—to seize your claim under the pretext of 'planetary security hazards.' Earth’s United Nations wants your Azra for their orbital defense platforms. And my government..." Vane paused, tapping a long finger on the steel desk. "...cannot allow either of them to monopolize it." Arthur felt a cold knot tighten in his stomach. "So I’m caught between corporate loan-sharks, an imperial Earth, and an expansionist star-system." "You are at the exact center of a galactic tug-of-war, Mr. Neegan," Vane agreed pleasantly. "If Trans-Martian Ore takes your land, they will process the Azra with indentured labor, reducing your fellow settlers to slaves. If Earth takes it, they will turn the Sol system into an impenetrable fortress, strangling interstellar trade. But Antares offers an alternative." Vane pulled a slim, illuminated data-slate from his drawer and slid it across the polished desk. Arthur looked down at the glowing text. "The offer," Vane said. "Transfer the Azra mineral titles to the Antares Sovereign Trust. In exchange, we transfer fifty million Sol-credits to a blind account on Titan. You will receive full diplomatic immunity, a high-ranking post on our scientific advisory board, and immediate evacuation." Arthur stared at the screen. The figure was staggering—enough to buy an entire orbital dome. But he knew how power worked. Nothing in the galaxy was given without a hidden cost. "And if I refuse?" Arthur asked quiet. Vane leaned back, his expression smoothing into a mask of polite indifference. "If you refuse, I land this shuttle back on your farm. Where Trans-Martian Ore's mercenaries will arrive before midnight. They will not offer you fifty million credits, Arthur. They will offer you a tragic equipment failure in an unmonitored airlock." Arthur looked out the viewscreen at Mars—a red marble hanging in the black, crisscrossed by the fragile, glowing domes of settlers who had sacrificed everything for autonomy. If he signed, he handed a super-weapon to an autocratic foreign power. If he refused, he died, and the corporations took it anyway. "You call this a choice, Director?" Arthur whispered. "I call it a gambit, Mr. Neegan," Vane replied, standing up. "And the board is already set. You have until we dock at the high-orbit station to decide which piece you intend to be."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully capturing Asimov's classic sci-fi style while delivering the requested scene structure. The author effectively establishes Arthur as a reluctant protagonist caught in galactic politics, using the transfer vessel setting to build tension before the crucial meeting with Director Vane. The worldbuilding is particularly strong, seamlessly integrating retrofuturistic elements (brass trim, phosphor-green monitors, teakwood paneling) with hard science fiction concepts. The Azra metal's properties are explained clearly without becoming overly technical, and the political implications are well-established through dialogue rather than exposition dumps. Character development shows nuance, particularly in Arthur's portrayal as an educated man playing ignorant while actually understanding the full implications of his situation. Vane emerges as a sophisticated antagonist who presents reasonable arguments while making veiled threats. The power dynamic between them feels authentic and creates genuine tension. The dialogue carries the story effectively, revealing character motivations and advancing the plot naturally. Vane's polished diplomatic language contrasts well with Arthur's more direct approach, and their conversation reveals the larger political stakes without feeling forced. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the "impossible choice" scenario and the ticking clock pressure are familiar tropes, though they're executed competently. The prose occasionally veers toward the overwrought, particularly in some descriptive passages, though it generally maintains appropriate restraint. The pacing works well, building from Arthur's discomfort through the revelation of stakes to the final ultimatum. The ending appropriately darkens the tone without feeling unearned, as Arthur's situation genuinely deteriorates throughout the scene. Technical execution is solid, with smooth sentence flow and consistent voice throughout. The piece maintains engagement through its combination of political intrigue, scientific concepts, and personal stakes. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The darkroom always feels detached from real time, but bathed in the heavy crimson of the safelight, it feels entirely detached from reality. The air is thick with the sharp, vinegary bite of stop bath and damp concrete. Outside, the university art building is locked down for the night; inside, it’s just the hum of the ventilation fan and the rhythmic, metallic sloshing of chemicals in plastic trays. Across the stainless-steel sink, Elliot sways slightly to an unheard rhythm. He’s nineteen, six years my junior, and effortlessly cool in a way that usually makes me want to roll my eyes. Tonight he’s wearing a sheer, frayed black mesh top over a worn thrifted tank, silver chains hanging heavy against his collarbones, his nails chipped with black polish. He moves with a quiet, fluid grace—a soft contrast to his sharp, killer nu-goth wardrobe. I’ve spent the whole semester watching him from across the studio. As a twenty-five-year-old senior with a reputation for taking up space, stepping into rooms boots-first, and directing my relationships like a stage manager, I’m not used to being captivated by someone so soft-spoken. Usually, my type is clear-cut: defined masculinity, assertive energy, people who know who they are and let me steer. But Elliot’s quiet intellect, his brilliant photographic eye, and the dreamy, blurred lines of his presence have been pulling at me for weeks. “This one came out too dark,” Elliot murmurs, his voice barely carrying over the exhaust fan. He uses wooden tongs to tilt a sheet of fiber paper in the developer tray. Under the red light, the emerging portrait looks like an oil slick, shadows devouring the subject's face. “You pushed the exposure three stops, El,” I say, stepping closer. My knee brushes the hem of his oversized skirt—a piece he layered over ripped denim tonight. “You need to pull it out early, or the shadows will just blow out.” My hand instinctively reaches to take the tongs from him, to fix it, to run the show like I always do. But as I reach, I see his fingers trembling. He drops the tongs into the tray with a soft splash. He doesn’t look at the print. He looks down at his boots, his dark, wavy hair falling like a curtain over his face. “Dani?” he asks, his voice barely a breath. I pause, pulling my hand back. “Yeah?” “Can I… tell you something? I haven’t really said it out loud yet.” The air in the darkroom instantly feels pressurized, the space shrinking around us. My usual instinct—to laugh, to make a bold joke, to take charge— evaporates. “Of course,” I say, keeping my tone grounded, softer than my usual bark. “I’m listening.” Elliot swallows hard. His fingers trace the dry edge of the sink counter. “I don’t think… I don’t think I’m a boy. At least, not the way everyone thinks I am. Or maybe not at all. I’m questioning… everything, honestly. How I want to look, how I want to exist. I feel like I’m constantly trying to develop a photo that isn’t coming out right because I’m using the wrong chemicals.” He gives a tiny, breathless chuckle at his own terrible metaphor, but his lower lip trembles. A sudden, sharp impulse hits me: I want to wrap him up, tell him it’s going to be fine, lay out a step-by-step plan for how he can explore this. I want to protect him from the world, from the awkwardness, from the fear evident in his tight shoulders. I open my mouth to take over, but I catch myself. *Don’t steamroll him, Dani.* This isn’t a project to manage. This is his space, his moment of stepping into the light. Taking the wheel right now would steal his agency just as he’s trying to claim it. “Thank you for telling me,” I say gently, fighting the urge to dictate the conversation. “How does it feel to say it?” Elliot looks up, dark eyes wide under the red glow. The safelight catches the subtle glitter on his cheekbones, the delicate structure of his jaw. “Terrifying,” he admits, a small, genuine smile breaking through his anxiety. “But… lighter. Like I’m finally stop-bathing a reaction that was going on too long.” Against my thigh, inside the pocket of my heavy denim jacket, my phone buzzes. Three long, muted vibrations. It’s probably my roommate wondering where I am, or some guy from Tinder replying to a message I sent three days ago. I don't care. I ignore the phantom pulse against my hip, refusing to break the sacred, insulated quiet of this red room. My mind is reeling, a chaotic mix of thrill and deep, unfamiliar confusion. Watching Elliot step tentatively into his true self is breathtaking. It’s an intimate privilege to be the one sitting in the dark with him while he finds his words. But underneath the protectiveness, there’s a sudden, warm coil of attraction that catches me off guard. I’m the girl who likes sharp edges and unambiguous lines. I’ve always understood my desire as something straight-edged, rooted in conventional dynamics where I play the irresistible, demanding force to a solid, masculine anchor. But standing here beside Elliot—as he unravels the very definition of who he is—I don’t feel turned off or confused about *him*. I feel electrified. The ambiguity isn't a wall; it's an expanse. His vulnerability is the sexiest thing I’ve ever seen. What does that mean for me? For my neat little categorizations of who I am and what I want? “You’re looking at me funny,” Elliot says softly, misinterpreting my silence. He steps back half an inch, wrapping his arms around himself. “Is it weird?” “No,” I say quickly, stepping forward to close the distance he just made. I reach out, taking his hand—not to push him, not to lead, but just to anchor us both. His skin is cool, damp with a stray drop of wash water. “It’s not weird at all, Elliot. It’s brave. And you look… remarkably yourself tonight.” Elliot breathes out, his shoulders dropping. He shifts his hand in mine, his fingers lacing through my heavy silver rings. The physical contact sends a jolt straight down my spine. The red light makes everything look flushed, high-contrast, exposed. “I didn’t know how you’d react,” he admits, staring down at our joined hands. “You always seem so… sure of everything. So confident.” “I’m good at faking it,” I reply, a sudden burst of honesty slipping past my guards. I step closer, until I can smell the sandalwood perfume sitting in the dip of his collarbone beneath the mesh. “Right now, I don’t feel sure of anything. Except that I really like being here with you.” Elliot glances up through his lashes, a flush creeping up his throat—darker even than the red light. The tender awkwardness hangs between us, thick and sweet. “Yeah?” he asks, a soft, dangerous spark in his voice. “Yeah,” I whisper. I let him make the next move, holding my breath, surrendering the lead for the first time in as long as I can remember. Elliot squeezes my hand, stepping firmly into my space, and for a long moment, we just stand there in the crimson hum, letting the image outline itself in the dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The author successfully creates an immersive darkroom setting that serves both as literal backdrop and metaphorical space for revelation and transformation. The red-light atmosphere is consistently maintained and effectively used to create intimacy and otherworldliness. The characterization of Dani is particularly well-executed. Her internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels authentic and creates genuine tension. The author skillfully shows her usual assertiveness being challenged and evolving in real-time, which creates character growth that feels earned rather than imposed. Her confusion about her own identity and attraction patterns adds layers of complexity that elevate the narrative beyond a simple coming-out story. Elliot's vulnerability is handled with sensitivity, and his tentative self-revelation feels genuine. The photography metaphors he uses ("trying to develop a photo that isn't coming out right because I'm using the wrong chemicals") work naturally within the setting and don't feel forced. The prose quality is generally high, with strong sensory details and effective use of the darkroom environment. The technical photography language is woven seamlessly into both dialogue and description. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from professional interaction to personal revelation to mutual attraction. However, there are some areas where the writing becomes slightly overwrought, particularly in describing physical details and internal sensations. Some metaphors, while thematically appropriate, occasionally feel heavy-handed. The ending, while sweet, edges toward being too neat given the complexity of the emotions and situations involved. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, capturing the tentative quality of the conversation without becoming stilted. The author successfully avoids making either character a mouthpiece for gender theory, instead focusing on personal, emotional truth. The piece succeeds in creating genuine emotional engagement and handles the subject matter with appropriate nuance and respect. The exploration of attraction and identity feels authentic rather than performative. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Scene I: The Screech of Trevi The high-pitched whine of a vintage Ducati echoed against the centuries-old travertine of the Piazza di Trevi. Ben, his nose buried deep in an annotated map of Imperial Rome, stepped off the curb directly into the path of a matte-black helmet. Rubber bit into cobblestone with an agonizing screech. The bike fishtailed, stopping an inch from Ben’s linen trousers. " *Ma sei pazzo?!* Are you trying to die today, or just ruin my suspension?" The rider swung a leg off the bike and ripped off her helmet. Dark curls tumbled over a leather jacket, revealing sharp brown eyes that burned with absolute, theatrical fury. Ben froze, his guidebook slipping from his fingers into a puddle. "I—oh, blimey. *Mi dispiace!* I mean, I am profoundly sorry. I was looking for the path to the aqueduct ruins and—" "You were looking at a piece of paper instead of a two-hundred-kilo vehicle," she snapped, stepping closer. She was half his size, but radiating enough energy to power the Roman grid. She picked up his dropped map, flicked the water off it, and handed it back. "I am Alessandra. And you are a walking hazard, *inglese*." "Ben," he managed, flushing crimson. "Dr. Benjamin Finch, actually. I’m on sabbatical—" "I don't care if you are the Pope," Alessandra interrupted, but the furious edge in her voice melted into a dangerous, dimpled grin. Her eyes flicked down to his jacket pocket, where a silver vintage fountain pen peeked out. In one fluid movement of impossible sleight-of-hand, she brushed past him to inspect her front tire, slipping the pen into her glove without him noticing. "You owe me an espresso for the wear on my brakes." Ben blinked, bewildered by the sudden shift. "I... suppose that’s fair." She threw him a spare helmet from the rear rack. "Put it on. Unless you prefer to walk through Rome getting run over by people less talented than me." *** ### Scene II: The Unsanctioned Tour Ben held on for dear life, his arms wrapped tightly around Alessandra’s waist as the Ducati slalomed through the labyrinthine alleys of Trastevere. Rome blurred past in a kaleidoscope of terracotta walls, hanging laundry, and sun-dappled plazas. He was terrified, but beneath his tweed-bound sensibilities, a strange, intoxicating hum of adrenaline began to sing in his veins. She pulled up outside a padlocked iron gate guarding a private 16th-century courtyard, completely off-limits to tourists. "Where are we?" Ben whispered as she produced a thin piece of wire from her pocket. "Alessandra, is that... are you picking a lock?" "I am opening a door," she corrected dryly. With a satisfying *click*, the gate swung open. "Come. The garden inside has a fountain made from a stolen sarcophagus. You like history, don't you?" "This is trespass! We could be arrested!" Ben stammered, yet his feet moved forward, drawn into her orbit like a moth to a flame. "Only if we stay long enough to chat with the *carabinieri*," she laughed, dragging him by the hand into the shaded sanctuary. As Ben stared in awe at the overgrown ivy and ancient marble, Alessandra lingered by a restorer’s cart parked near a marble bust. While Ben’s back was turned, her fingers danced over a tray of antique terracotta mosaic shards. She selected a small, azure-glazed piece—a fragment of Renaissance sky—and pocketed it with practiced grace. She turned to Ben, who was watching her with a mixture of terror and utter fascination. "You're mad," he breathed, a smile tugging uncontrollably at the corner of his lips. "Completely, wonderfully mad." "And you are boring, Dr. Benjamin," she countered, stepping uncomfortably close, reaching up to adjust his askew collar. Her fingers brushed his throat, sending a violent shiver down his spine. "I am doing you a favor. I am making you alive." *** ### Scene III: The Deluge at the Gelateria By four in the afternoon, the Mediterranean blue of the sky disintegrated into a bruised, dramatic violet. A sudden summer downpour broke over the city, fat drops hammering the pavement with heavy rhythm. Alessandra grabbed Ben’s wrist, pulling him under the striped canvas awning of *Gelateria del Teatro*. The air turned cool and smelled of damp earth, espresso, and roasted pistachios. They stood shoulder-to-shoulder, drenched, listening to the rain turn the cobblestones into shimmering mirrors. "Well," Ben panted, wringing out the hem of his jacket. "This was not in the itinerary." Alessandra leaned against the glass display case, her dark eyes gleaming as she watched him. "Itineraries are for people who are afraid of surprises." "I used to like predictability," Ben admitted, stepping closer to avoid the runoff dripping from the awning's edge. He was mere inches from her now, consumed by the smell of rain and her floral perfume. "Then I stepped in front of your motorcycle." Alessandra leaned in, her voice dropping to a seductive whisper. "And now?" "Now I think my itinerary was utterly rubbish." She laughed, a rich, dark sound, and reached into her jacket. "Hold out your hand." Ben obeyed. She dropped the azure mosaic tile into his palm. His jaw dropped. "Alessandra! This is from the garden! You stole it!" "I liberated it," she corrected mischievously. "Consider it a souvenir. A piece of Rome you didn't have to read about in a book." Ben stared at the smooth, ancient tile, then at the woman standing before him—a whirlwind of chaos, beauty, and crime. He should have been horrified. Instead, his heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird. *** ### Scene IV: Stolen Moments Dusk fell, painting the skyline in hues of magenta and gold as the rain receded into a soft mist. They stood atop the Pincio Hill, looking out over the glowing expanse of Piazza del Popolo. "I have to return to my flat," Alessandra said softly, leaning back against the stone balustrade. For the first time all day, her manic energy slowed to a gentle, enigmatic simmer. "My shift starts early tomorrow." Ben felt a sudden, sharp pang of panic. The day was ending, and with it, the fever dream. "Will I... see you again?" Alessandra stepped forward. She reached into her pocket and pulled out his silver fountain pen, twirling it between her fingers before sliding it back into his breast pocket. Ben blinked. "My pen? How on earth—" "I told you," she whispered, stepping onto her tiptoes. "I am a troublemaker." She placed a hand on the back of his neck, pulling him down, and pressed her lips to his. The kiss was brief, electric, and tasted of wild strawberry gelato and rain. When she pulled back, Ben was entirely breathless, completely disoriented, and hopelessly smitten. Alessandra slid her helmet back on, her eyes crinkling behind the visor with secret delight. She swung her leg over the Ducati, revved the engine, and winked at him. "Check your watch, *inglese*," she called out over the roar of the engine. Ben looked down at his bare wrist. His watch was gone. "If you want it back," Alessandra shouted with a dazzling laugh, kicking the bike into gear, "be at the Trevi Fountain tomorrow morning at eight. Don't be late!" With a flash of red taillights, she vanished into the Roman night, leaving Ben standing in the twilight, laughing like a madman into the damp, ancient air.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through action and dialogue. Alessandra's mischievous energy and Ben's scholarly awkwardness are well-established and consistently maintained throughout. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The synth-amber lighting behind the bar hums with a comfortable, low-frequency buzz that I usually feel in my molars by midnight. Out here on the Andromeda outer rim, *The Last Outpost* isn’t much to look at—just a hollowed-out nickel asteroid stuffed with recycled air, cheap booze, and bad decisions. But it’s mine. Or close enough to it. "I’m telling you, Nets, the core drill on the *Rusty Pick* is humming in G-minor," Barnaby grumbles, slamming his heavy, three-fingered fist onto the scarred brass counter. "That means the dampener is shot. Dead. Toast." "Or it means you left your audio tuner on the wrong frequency again, Barns," I say, pouring a splash of green synth-ale into his glass. "Like last Tuesday." "It’s G-minor! I know a dying dampener when I hear one!" Across the bar, Lyra—a blue-skinned cartographer with a penchant for heartbreakers—leans over her glowing datapads and snorts. "He’s not mad about the drill, Nets. He’s upset because Sarah down on Dock B wouldn't accept his hydro-carrots." "They were organic!" Barnaby huffs, his graying eyebrows knitting together. "Grown in pure, composted asteroid dust!" "She’s allergic to dirt, Barns," I gently remind him, sliding his glass toward him. "She told you that when you tried to give her those space-radishes last month. Try synthesized flowers next time. Less... earthy." Barnaby mutters something under his breath about the modern dating scene being ruined by sterile hydroponics, but he takes a long gulp of his ale anyway. I smile, picking up a rag to wipe down the taps. I love this nonsense. Back in my old life—before I ditched my real name, my debts, and a rather furious syndicate boss—a loud room meant someone was drawing a blaster. Here, a loud room just means the local ice-miners are arguing over jukebox tracks. My flaws are many—I’m paranoid, I pocket forgotten coins, and I’m far too fond of meddling in other people's business—but out here, those flaws make me a damn good bartender. The station’s artificial gravity gives its usual lazy hiccup. Around the lounge, half-empty mugs slosh in unison. The green ale in Barnaby’s glass wobbles dangerously, rising in a slow, thick wave against the rim before settling back down. "Fixer-upper of a station," Lyra sighs, catching her leaning datapad before it slides into a bowl of salted nut-pods. "The grav-plates in Sector Four are acting up again. I nearly floated out of my bunk this morning." "I'll bug the chief engineer tomorrow," I say. "If he ever finishes his second glass of plum wine." "He won't," Lyra chuckles. "He's currently trying to build up the courage to ask out the new cargo loader." "Ooh, the tall one with the third eye?" I lean in, resting my elbows on the brass rail. "I give them three days. They have zero shared interests, but the tension in the breakroom is practically a fire hazard." "I put twenty credits on them lasting a month," Lyra says, grinning. "Care to take the bet, Nets?" "You know I don't gamble with patrons," I say, winking. "It’s unethical. Plus, I already know how it ends." Before Lyra can negotiate the odds, the heavy pneumatic airlock doors at the edge of the bar hiss open. It’s an ugly, wet sound that doesn't fit the usual cadence of our late-night regulars. A draft of stale, ozone-heavy air sweeps through the room, carrying the sharp, metallic stink of a fried hyperdrive. The chatter in the bar dips for a brief second, then resumes its lazy murmur. But my eyes are already locked on the doorway. Old habits die hard. The newcomer stumbles into the warm light of the bar, brushing past a booth of laughing drillers. They are Ceph-kin, an aquatic species rarely seen this far out toward the void. Their tentacled dreads, usually kept neatly oiled and pinned, are tangled and hanging askew over their shoulders. Dark, iridescent grease stains their heavy flight coat, alongside scorched marks that look terrifyingly like fresh plasma burns. They drag their feet toward the counter, ignoring the empty booths, and quietly plop down at the stool right in front of me. "Vega whisky, neat," the stranger says, voice raspy, dry, and breathless. "Better make that a double." I don't ask for a chip or an ID. I just reach beneath the bar and pull down the heavy, indigo-glass bottle of Vega dark. I pour two generous fingers into a heavy crystal glass. Just as I set it down, the station gravity flickers again—a harder jitter this time. The deep purple whisky wobbles violently, a droplet detaching from the surface and floating half an inch into the air before snapping back into the glass. "Station's grav-plates are cranky tonight," I say softly, keeping my tone warm, easy, bartender-friendly. "I'm Nets. Welcome to *The Last Outpost*. You look like you just dodged a solar flare." The stranger grabs the glass with trembling, suction-cupped fingers and downs the shot in a single, desperate gulp. They wince as it hits their throat, their tentacled dreads twitching in tight, nervous knots against their neck. "I wish it was a solar flare," they whisper, dark black eyes darting toward the airlock doors, then down at their trembling hands. "Bad run through the Belt?" I ask, leaning a fraction closer, dropping my voice below the swell of the jukebox. "No," the stranger rasps. They lean across the counter, the stench of burnt copper and pure adrenaline radiating off them. "They tracked me." My easy bartender smile falters, the muscle in my jaw tightening. "Who's 'they'?" "The Iron Fleet," the stranger breathes, their dark eyes locking onto mine with absolute terror. "I slipped their blockade at Sector Nine. But my drive died when I hit your orbit. They're right behind me." Down the counter, Barnaby slams his glass again. "Nets! Gravity’s slipping! Pour me another before my ale floats off!" I don't move. My ears catch a low, terrifying rumble echoing through the station’s outer hull—a deep, heavy thump that has nothing to do with the asteroid belt or faulty grav-plates. Through the thick plas-glass observation window behind the bar, out in the pitch-black void, a massive, unlit silhouette slowly blocks out the distant stars. "Nets?" Barnaby asks, his voice suddenly losing its booming confidence. "What is that?" The Ceph-kin looks up at me, their tentacles curling in tight, helpless coils. "I have something in my ship's cargo hold," they whisper. "Something they will burn this entire rock to the ground to get back." The bar’s lights flicker, dying down to a dull, emergency red. The whisky in the bottle on my counter wobbles, floating upward in a slow, suspended sphere.

The dialogue flows naturally and serves multiple purposes - character development, exposition, and atmosphere building. Character actions feel believable throughout. Nets responds as an experienced bartender would - observant, welcoming, but cautious. Her past as someone fleeing trouble makes her immediate recognition of danger credible. The stranger's desperation and fear come through clearly in their dialogue and physical descriptions. The prose strikes a good balance between descriptive and functional, avoiding purple prose while maintaining atmospheric detail. Descriptions like "tentacled dreads askew" and "stench of burnt copper and pure adrenaline" are vivid without being overwrought. The writing maintains consistent voice and tone throughout. Some minor weaknesses include occasional reliance on familiar sci-fi tropes (mysterious cargo, pursuing fleet) and a few moments where exposition feels slightly forced. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The top right corner of my cracked phone screen glows with a bitter little truth: 12%. No charger, no outline of a plan, and no way back. Not that I’d go back anyway. The beat-up Ford pickup that picked me up outside of Memphis pulled over on Canal Street half an hour ago. The driver, a guy named Earl who smelled like menthols and stale coffee, took one look at my oversized hoodie and mess of dyed hair, spit out his window, and said, *“This is as far as you go, kid. Welcome to the Big Easy.”* Then he drove off, leaving me standing on the hot, sticky asphalt. The air in New Orleans doesn't breathe; it clings. It wraps around your throat like a wet towel. *Concerning behavioural patterns.* That’s what Mr. Henderson, the high school guidance counsellor, called me on the phone to my mother last month. *“Taylor has a habit of inventing drama to escape reality.”* I let out a bitter, silent laugh that turns into a cough. Inventing drama. Right. Because coming out to my parents forty-eight hours ago was just a casual little theater production. I can still see Mom’s face—the sudden, terrifying drop in her expression, the way her eyes went flat and cold when the words *I’m trans* left my mouth. Dad hadn't even yelled. He’d just stood up, turned off the TV, and walked out of the house. The silence that followed was louder than any screaming match. It was a eviction notice signed in shadow. So yeah, I executed my escape plan last night in thirty flat minutes. A backpack, eighty-four dollars in crumpled cash stolen from my own birthday stash, and a jump out the bathroom window while they were at evening service. Now I’m here. I wander down Decatur Street, my sneakers squeaking against the pavement. Everything is too loud, too bright, too much. Brass bands are blasting on street corners, tourists are drinking red slushies out of giant plastic yards, and the smell of fried dough and sewage hangs in the air. I am completely, utterly free. And I have never been so terrified in my life. I drop onto a stone bench near Jackson Square, pulling my knees to my chest. I check my phone again. 9%. *Turn it off,* my brain screams. *Save it for an emergency.* *Who are you going to call in an emergency?* another voice whispers back. *Mom? The counsellor? You don’t exist to them anymore.* "You're gonna wreck your posture sitting like that." I flinch, my head snapping up. Standing a few feet away is a girl—or maybe a guy, or somewhere in between—wearing a ripped army jacket that’s way too big for them, cut-off denim shorts, and heavy black boots despite the suffocating heat. They’ve got a dark, jagged pixie cut, skin the color of toasted almonds, and a vicious purple bruise blossoming across their left jawline. I pull my hoodie tighter around myself, feeling instantly defensive. "I'm fine." The kid snorts, taking a bite out of a powdery, square pastry. "Yeah, you look great. Nothing says 'I'm thriving' like a kid sweating to death in a winter coat while staring at a dead cell phone like it's a bomb." They toss the bag of pastries into my lap. "Eat. You look like a ghost." I stare at the bag. Powdered sugar clings to the wax paper. "I don't have money to pay you for this." "Didn't ask for money," they say, sliding onto the bench next to me with an easy, fluid grace. "Name's Mars. They/them, or whatever. What’s yours?" "Taylor," I mutter. "They/them too." My voice trips over the pronouns. It’s the first time I’ve said them out loud to someone who isn't staring at me like I’m a broken toaster. It feels weird. Good, but weird. Mars tilts their head, evaluating me with sharp, dark eyes. "Well, Taylor-They-Them, you got 'runaway' tattooed across your forehead in bright pink neon. Where’d you slide in from?" "Tennessee," I say softly. "Middle of nowhere." "Ah. Land of corn and judgment." Mars chuckles, but there’s no warmth in it. They glance over their shoulder, their gaze scanning the crowd in Jackson Square—slow, deliberate, paranoid. "You got a place to crash?" "Working on it," I lie. "Right. So you're sleeping on a stoop tonight unless the cops haul you to a shelter." Mars digs into their jacket pocket and pulls out a crushed pack of cigarettes, flipping it open. "Word of advice? Stay away from the riverfront after dark. And if anyone offers you a 'free place to stay' near the Quarter, tell 'em to rot in hell. This city eats soft kids like you for breakfast." I glare at them, a sudden flare of my old, defensive anger rising up. "I'm not soft." "You're wearing a fleece hoodie in ninety-degree humidity, Taylor. You're practically melting." Mars sparks a lighter, lighting a cigarette down to the filter. "We're all soft until the pavement hardens us." I watch the smoke curl up into the humid afternoon air. I want to ask about the bruise on their face. I want to ask what's weighing down the bottom of their oversized army pack, which clunks heavily against the stone bench every time they move—something solid, metallic, and distinctly un-kid-like. I want to ask who they keep looking for in the crowd. But I know the rules of the road, even if I only joined twenty-four hours ago: *Don't ask questions you don't want to answer yourself.* "Why did you leave?" I ask instead, keeping it general. Mars takes a long drag, staring out at the steeples of St. Louis Cathedral. For a second, the street-smart armor slips, revealing a raw, exhausted kid underneath. "Creative differences," Mars says dryly. "My stepdad thought he could hit the gay out of me. I thought I'd hit him with a heavy brass lamp and steal his truck." My heart leaps into my throat. "You stole a truck?" "Ditch-landed it in Alabama," Mars replies with a smirk, but their fingers are trembling slightly around the cigarette. "Secrets keep you alive, Tennessee. Remember that." We sit in silence for an hour as the sun begins to sink, painting the sky in violent shades of bruised orange and deep purple. New Orleans is shifting gears, the day crowd fading into the darker, slicker energy of the night. My phone buzzes in my hand. One single, desperate vibrate. *Battery at 2%.* I flip it over. A missed text from Mom from six hours ago: *Please call us, Taylor. You're making a mistake.* Is it a mistake? Panic hits me like a freight train, cold and heavy. I'm sixteen years old. I have seventy-two dollars, a dying phone, no home, and my only companion is a runaway who might be a felon. I could go back. I could call the counsellor. I could pretend I never said anything, swallow myself down, and go back to being the miserable, quiet ghost in the hallway. Mars stands up, slinging their heavy backpack over one shoulder. They look down at me, holding out a hand dusted with powdered sugar. "Night's coming," Mars says. "I know a squat near the Marigny. It's safe-ish. You coming, or are you going to sit there and cry into your phone?" I look at my screen. 1%. Then, black. The screen goes dark. The tether is cut. There is no going back. There’s only forward, into the dark, hot streets of a city that doesn't care if I live or die—but where, for the first time in my life, I am finally completely myself. I take Mars's hand and pull myself up. "Lead the way," I say.

The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor feels authentically sixteen - vulnerable yet defiant, scared but trying to project toughness. Their internal voice captures the complexity of someone dealing with rejection, fear, and newfound freedom simultaneously. Mars is equally well-developed as a street-smart runaway with their own secrets and trauma, creating an interesting dynamic without falling into stereotypes. The prose quality is generally high, with vivid sensory details that bring New Orleans to life. Descriptions like "The air in New Orleans doesn't breathe; it clings" and the contrast between tourist brightness and underlying danger effectively establish atmosphere. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. Dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, revealing character through speech patterns and word choices. Mars's street-smart cynicism contrasts well with Taylor's more sheltered background, and their conversation flows organically while advancing both plot and character development. The emotional complexity is handled skillfully. Taylor's conflicting feelings about their escape - terror mixed with relief, loneliness alongside newfound freedom - feel genuine rather than overwrought. The piece doesn't shy away from the real dangers these characters face while maintaining hope. The pacing works well, moving from Taylor's immediate disorientation through their meeting with Mars to the symbolic moment of the phone dying. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - Taylor makes a choice to move forward, but the uncertainty and danger remain real. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly heavy-handed, and a few descriptions that edge toward being overwrought. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The world had not ended with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a series of blue-screen error messages and a deeply regretful email from customer support that no one had lived to read. Now, two centuries into the After, humanity was reduced to scavengers, philosophers, and people like Midas, who fell firmly into the category of "those who trip over things that were previously impossible to trip over." Midas sat on an upside-down bucket of spackle, staring at a grease-stained map of the local *Wal-Em-Mart*. Across from him, balanced precariously on a stack of extinct tax software manuals, sat Chewy. Chewy was an animatronic koala manufactured during the late Capitalocene by a company whose motto had reportedly been *“Why spend money on love when you can buy synthetic acrylic?”* Chewy possessed a degraded, nuclear-powered heart—the kind once put in cheap novelty toys designed to survive a direct artillery hit—and a set of fiber-optic eyes that reacted to internal stress levels by changing color. Currently, Chewy’s eyes were a dull, stagnant yellow. The color of mild, ambient despair. "The strategy is simple," Midas said, tapping a soot-stained thumbnail against the map. "We breach the North entrance—what the ancients called *Lawn & Garden*. We skirt Aisle Four, secure the prize, and retreat before the sun hits the horizon." Chewy’s left eye flickered a faint, pulse-like violet. Existential dread. "I know," Midas admitted, leaning back until his spine popped. "Aisle Four is bad. Aisle Four is where the floor tiles came up in the Great Thaw. But the prize, Chewy... the prize is a sealed tin of *Spam*. Real meat. Or, at least, the salt-cured promise of something that once stood near a pig." Chewy’s eyes shifted to a pale, skeptical green. "It’s not a trap," Midas insisted, adjusting his scrap-metal elbow guard, which was actually a rusted hubcap held together by prayer and zip-ties. "I scouted it yesterday. The squatter-gulls have moved south. The floor-sweeping automations are dead. It’s a ghost town. An easy run." Chewy’s eyes flickered orange. Warning. Midas ignored it. Midas had a long, distinguished history of ignoring orange lights. *** Forty minutes later, they were inside the Megamart. The air smelled of damp plaster, dead leaves, and the peculiar, everlasting scent of cheap carpet. Sunlight speared through holes in the corrugated roof, illuminating floating motes of dust that had been orbiting the ruin since the collapse of the global banking system. "See?" Midas whispered, stepping carefully over a petrified bag of potting soil. "Quiet as a grave." He reached Aisle Four. There, resting upon the third shelf of a battered display unit—glowing beneath a stray beam of sunlight like an artifact of immense, forbidden divinity—was the tin of Spam. It was dented, covered in a fine patina of forty-year-old dust, but unbroken. Midas held his breath. He took a step forward. His boot met a loose floor tile. The tile, which had been waiting forty years for a victim of precise weight and poor spatial awareness, tilted instantly. Midas’s ankle turned with a sickening *pop*. He lunged forward to catch himself, his hands slapping full-force against the metal shelving. The entire unit—a twelve-foot-tall monolith of steel and long-decayed cookware—groaned. *“Caution,”* a tinny, synthesized voice suddenly warbled from a speaker in the ceiling. *“You have entered a restricted area. Please wait for an associate to assist you with your purchase.”* Chewy, perched safely in Midas’s coat pocket, immediately lit up like a neon road sign. His eyes strobed a violent, blinding crimson—the universal animatronic code for pure, unadulterated panic. "Chewy, turn it off!" Midas hissed, scrambling up on one good leg. The crimson glow reflected off a shattered mirror on the floor, bouncing directly into the dusk of Aisle Five. From Aisle Five came a low, mechanical hum, followed by the terrifying *clack-clack-clack* of rubberized treads on cracked linoleum. It was a *Floor-Vac 5000*. It had lost its dustbin in the late 2030s, replaced its cleaning routines with a corrupted loop of violent territorialism, and welded a rusty meat cleaver to its front bumper during some forgotten gang war among the appliances. "Run," Midas squeaked. He turned to bolt, forgot about his sprained ankle, and immediately fell flat on his face. Chewy slid out of his pocket, tumbling across the aisle and stopping neatly at the base of the charging Floor-Vac. Chewy’s eyes flashed bright, luminous pink—a emotion the manual had once defined as *“Overwhelming Joy,”* but in this context clearly meant *“My microchips are short-circuiting from mortal terror.”* The robot paused, its optical sensors locking onto the glowing pink stuffed animal. It whirred, confused by the sudden disco ball in its path. Midas, operating entirely on adrenaline and bad judgment, grabbed the nearest weapon—a three-foot bar of solid rusted rebar—and swung it like a golf club. He missed the robot entirely, hit the support beam of the shelf above him, and brought thirty-four tins of expired, waterlogged dog food down directly onto his own head. *** The return journey was not a march; it was a slow, degrading crawl of shame. They reached the hovel just as the sun dipped beneath the jagged skyline of the old world. Midas collapsed through the doorway, sliding onto the dirt floor with a wet thud. He took stock of his physical inventory. He had: 1. One sprained right ankle (bad). 2. A swelling knot on his forehead the size and shape of a plum (worse). 3. A missing left shoe, lost somewhere in the violent gears of a Floor-Vac 5000 (disastrous). 4. A jacket that was now forty percent wasp stings, courtesy of a nest he had disturbed while crawling through the Garden Center exit. He turned his head slowly. Beside him sat Chewy. The koala had lost a significant patch of synthetic fur from his left flank, his ear was permanently bent at a ninety-degree angle, and his internal speaker was emitting a faint, steady whistle like a teapot on a low flame. Midas reached into his shredded coat pocket and pulled out their prize. He stared at it in the dimming twilight. It was not Spam. In the blind panic beneath the cascading dog food, Midas’s hand had snatched the wrong vessel. He was now the proud owner of a twelve-ounce glass jar of *Marinated Artichoke Hearts*, best consumed by May 2014. Midas closed his eyes. "We almost died for salad, Chewy." Chewy sat in the dark dirt. Slowly, his fiber-optic eyes shifted from the frantic crimson of battle, past the sickly green of doubt, and settled into a soft, glowing, contented cerulean blue. *Satisfaction.* Midas sighed, reached for his improvised bottle opener, and leaned back against the dirt wall. "Tomorrow," Midas muttered, popping the seal on the jar, "we go for the batteries." Chewy’s eyes flickered orange, just once, and then went dark.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, observational humor, and ability to find profound absurdity in mundane situations. The opening line about the world ending with blue-screen errors immediately establishes the Pratchettesque tone, blending technological collapse with bureaucratic banality. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believable post-apocalyptic everyman whose defining trait—finding trouble in impossible situations—drives both plot and humor naturally. The animatronic koala Chewy is brilliantly conceived, with his color-coded emotional states serving as both exposition device and running gag. The relationship between them feels genuine despite the absurd premise. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with memorable phrases like "the salt-cured promise of something that once stood near a pig" and "forty percent wasp stings" that capture Pratchett's gift for unexpected metaphors. The world-building is economical but vivid, creating a believable post-technological landscape through selective details. The story structure follows the requested format perfectly: setup, mission gone wrong, return home worse for wear. The escalating disasters feel organic rather than forced, each mishap flowing logically from character flaws and environmental hazards. The Floor-Vac 5000 is a particularly inspired antagonist, embodying the story's theme of technology gone feral. However, the piece occasionally veers toward over-description, particularly in the inventory sequences. Some metaphors, while clever, border on purple prose. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels slightly rushed compared to the careful buildup of the middle section. The dialogue is minimal but effective when present, mostly consisting of Midas's internal monologue and his one-sided conversations with Chewy. This works well for the story's tone and avoids the pitfall of forced banter. The emotional core—two unlikely companions making the best of an impossible world—resonates without becoming sentimental. The final moment of shared satisfaction over expired artichoke hearts perfectly captures the story's theme of finding contentment in small victories amid larger failures. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The brass bell above the heavy oak door chimed frantically as the man practically threw himself inside, slamming the latch shut behind him. Rain splattered against the glass in a thick Cardiff drizzle, blurring the figures hovering on the cobbles of Castle Arcade with flashbulbs at the ready. Julian Croft leaned his back against the glass, chest heaving beneath an absurdly expensive, drenched cashmere coat. He pushed his dark, wet curls back from his face, took a theatrical breath, and looked up, instantly turning on the half-smirk that had graced three dozen magazine covers this year alone. "Tell me you have a secret trapdoor, a rear exit, or at least a very large, opaque curtain," Julian said, his voice dropping into that rich, velvet baritone that usually made interviewers melt on spot. "Because if those vultures get a shot of my hair looking like a drowned rat, my publicist will have a stroke." Behind the polished mahogany counter, Carys didn't even look up from her ledger immediately. She dipped her fountain pen into an inkwell, blotted a line, and finally raised her eyes. "Browsing or buying?" she asked dryly. Her accent was pure Cardiff—crisp, grounded, and entirely unimpressed. "Because if you’re planning on dripping on the rare poetry section, the answer is 'neither', and the door is right behind you." Julian paused. The smirk faltered for a fraction of a second—a micro-glitch in his carefully cultivated aura of effortless magnetism. He slid his hood down entirely, stepping into the warm amber light of the shop, tilting his chin so the chandelier caught his jawline. It was a movement he’d practiced in mirrors since he was nineteen. "Julian," he offered, holding out a hand, giving her a look of soft, intimate conspirator. "Julian Croft. But you can call me whatever you like, provided it ends with 'saving my life'." Carys looked at his extended hand, then up at his face. Her heart gave a sudden, treacherous thud against her ribs. Up close, he was infuriatingly beautiful—all sharp angles, dark, storm-grey eyes, and a scent of rain and expensive sandalwood. *Hold it together,* she told herself firmly. *He’s an actor. He gets paid to make people look at him like that.* "Right then," she said, returning to her ledger. "‘Nuisance’ it is. Step off the Persian rug, Nuisance. You’re ruining the weave." Julian withdrew his hand, a sharp sting of disbelief piercing his ego. *Nuisance?* He looked down at the rug, then back at her. Was she blind? Was she joking? He looked for a hint of a smile, a flutter of eyelashes, the inevitable flush of a fan trying to play it cool. But Carys was calmly re-capping her pen. "Ouch," Julian said, though he forced a light, roguish laugh to cover the slight wobble in his confidence. "Usually people ask for a selfie before they kick me out into the tempest." "I only sign receipts," Carys replied, keeping her voice strictly professional, though her fingers trembled slightly as she closed the book. "And the tempest is just a typical Cardiff Tuesday. They’ll clear off once they realize there’s no story here." Julian stepped closer to the counter, leaning one forearm against it, deliberately invading her space with a slow, devastating smile. "Come now. A world-famous actor taking shelter in a charming, dusty little bookshop with a fiercely guarded owner? That’s practically a narrative arc in itself. You aren't... *unaffected* by my plight, are you?" He leaned in just a fraction more, his voice dropping an octave, warm and heavy with suggestion. It was his signature move—the one that had swept through costume dramas and modern thrillers alike. Carys felt a heat creep up her neck, straight to the tips of her ears. Her pulse rattled in her throat. He was infuriatingly good at this. But there was something about the subtle desperation beneath his polished veneer—the sharp, hungry way his eyes searched her face for validation—that gave her courage. She turned her gaze slowly to meet his, raising one dark eyebrow. "Mr. Croft," she said evenly, "I run an antiquarian bookshop in a Victorian arcade. The most dramatic thing that happened here today was a silverfish in the 19th-century geography shelf. I assure you, your hair is very low on my list of concerns." Julian’s jaw actually slackened. He blinked. He dropped his arm from the counter, straightening up as if he'd been slapped with a cold flounder. *She genuinely doesn't care,* he thought, horrified and utterly fascinated. *Or she thinks I'm a terrible actor. Or worse... mediocre.* The fragile, intricate tower of his self-esteem wobbled ominously. But right behind the ego-bruise came a sudden, sharp jolt of genuine heat in his chest. He looked at her properly now—not as an audience to be conquered, but as a person. She had sharp, intelligent hazel eyes, a faint smattering of freckles across her nose, and a stubborn set to her jaw that made his breath catch. "You're... terribly mean," Julian murmured. The rehearsed charm vanished, replaced by an authentic, bewildered curiosity. He took a step back, sweeping a hand through his damp hair without a care for how it looked. "Is it me? Or do you just hate cinema in general?" "I love cinema," Carys said, her voice softening just a fraction, though she kept her defensive posture. "I just don't particularly care for men who expect a red carpet spread out over my floorboards." "I didn't expect a red carpet!" Julian protested, a genuine laugh bubbling up from his chest—not his smooth press-junket chuckle, but a raspy, surprised sound. "A dry towel, perhaps. A hot cup of tea, at a stretch. But not a verbal execution!" Carys fought a sudden, overwhelming urge to smile. It was a losing battle; the corner of her mouth twitched upward. *God help me,* she thought, *he's actually endearing when he isn't trying so hard.* "Tea is for paying customers," she said softly. Julian leaned back over the counter, but this time the arrogance was gone, replaced by a spark of pure, playful challenge. The intensity in his grey eyes was real now, focused entirely on her. "Name your price," he said quietly, his voice humming with an unspoken electricity that made the air between them feel suddenly thick, almost heavy. "I'll buy the whole shop if it gets me ten minutes of your time without the sarcasm." "The sarcasm is non-negotiable," Carys countered, her breathing growing shallow as he held her gaze. "And the shop isn't for sale." "Then sell me a book," Julian whispered, his eyes dipping to her lips for a fraction of a second before darting back to her eyes. "Pick one out for me. Something that proves you don't completely despise me." Carys reached beneath the counter, her hands absurdly shaky, and pulled out a worn, leather-bound volume of Dylan Thomas. She slid it across the wood between them until her fingers brushed his. A tiny spark seemed to leap between their skin, and both of them stilled. "Ten pounds," she murmured, unable to look away from him. Julian didn't look at the book. He kept his eyes locked on hers, a slow, genuine smile spreading across his face—one that had nothing to do with Hollywood, and everything to do with the quiet, rain-slicked room they were sharing. "Bargain," he said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates a meet-cute scenario in a Welsh bookstore with two well-defined characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue and action. The characterization is particularly effective. Julian is portrayed as a charming but insecure actor whose practiced magnetism falters when met with genuine indifference, revealing vulnerability beneath his polished exterior. Carys is equally well-drawn as someone genuinely unimpressed by celebrity but not immune to authentic connection. The author skillfully shows both characters' internal states while maintaining their distinct voices. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with each character having a recognizable speech pattern - Julian's theatrical, practiced charm versus Carys's dry, grounded Welsh directness. The banter feels natural and serves character development while advancing the romantic tension. The Welsh setting is well-integrated through specific details like Castle Arcade and Cardiff references, though it could have been more deeply embedded. The bookshop atmosphere is convincingly rendered with tactile details like the fountain pen, inkwell, and Persian rug. The romantic chemistry builds believably through their verbal sparring, with the author showing rather than telling the attraction through physical reactions and behavioral changes. Julian's transformation from performative charm to genuine interest feels earned rather than sudden. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose, particularly in descriptions of Julian's appearance and movements. Some metaphors feel overwrought ("verbal execution," "cold flounder"). The pacing is generally strong, though a few moments of internal monologue slow the momentum slightly. The ending strikes an appropriate note of romantic possibility without rushing into unrealistic territory. The symbolic exchange of the Dylan Thomas book provides a satisfying conclusion that honors both characters' intelligence and the Welsh setting. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Aya pushed the iron-reinforced door inward. The heavy brass hinges groaned, a sound that grated brutally against the damp silence of the underhold. Inside, the air hung thick with the pungent, sweet stench of burning leviathan tallow. The flickering gas lamps cast long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor—shadows that stretched like reaching, translucent fingers toward the vault at the far end, where the Scythan artifact rested beneath its dormant wards. There were no guards unconscious on the flagstones. There was no sign of a desperate breach. Instead, sitting comfortably upon a brass-bound shipping crate beneath the sputtering green light of an oil sconce, sat Mother Vane. She was decidedly un-incarcerated. Her double-breasted leather coat was spotless, its polished brass buttons gleaming in the dismal light. In her gloved hand rested a fine, twin-barreled pistol with a stock carved from whale-bone. "Looking for the crown jewels, little crows?" Vane’s voice rattled like gravel dragged across an iron grate. Before Simeon could draw his bone-handled dirk, or Katra could reach for her blubber-hook, the darkness along the stone walls unraveled. Six men stepped out from the deep alcoves—heavy-set harpooners carrying spring-loaded brass crossbows, their heavy bolts tipped with black-powder caps. The loud, metallic *clack-clack* of cocking mechanisms echoed off the dripping vault. "Drop 'em," Simeon muttered, his voice cracking as he froze. "Aya, we're boxed." Aya felt a cold, prickling sweat break out beneath her velvet hood. Deep within her chest, the immateria stirred—a bitter, subterranean cold yearning to tear through the veil and summon something jagged and hungry from the dark to rend these men to flinders. But iron surrounded them, and brass, and cold whale-oil. A single flicker of immateria sparks would draw six bolts through their ribcages before her shadow-beasts could fully manifest. *Men in this city trust brass and steel,* Aya reminded herself, her heart hammering wildly against her ribs. *They do not hesitate to shoot what terrifies them.* Slowly, Katra and Simeon dropped their weapons to the stones. Two burly thugs surged forward, forcing the trio to their knees. Heavy iron manacles were slammed onto Aya’s wrists, locking with a dull, sickening clink that cut off the subtle flow of her magick like a cold tourniquet. Vane stepped down from the crate, her iron-shod boots clicking rhythmically against the stone. She approached Aya, reaching out with a gloved hand to seize the edge of Aya's silk mask. With a sharp, contemptuous tug, the fabric ripped away. Aya blinked against the harsh tallow light. Her sharp, pale features, dark eyes, and unblemished skin were laid bare—a stark, absurd contrast to the grease-stained, scarred faces of the guild. "Well, well," Vane purred, leaning in until Aya could smell the bitter gin and sea-salt on her breath. "The mysterious shadow-caster of the Docks. I took you for a gutter-born witch from the Rips. But look at those cheekbones. That skin’s never known a day’s hard labor, nor the reek of the rendering-vats." Katra gasped from the floor beside her. "Aya?" Aya kept her expression locked into a mask of aristocratic ice, even as panic threatened to drown her. The truth was out. If Vane realized who she truly was, the nightmare wouldn't merely end with her swinging from a gibbet; it would drag down her father, her house, her very memory. Her father, Lord Vance, would disown her posthumously—or hand her to the High Inquisitors himself to save his own seat on the Admiralty Board, just as he had turned a blind eye when her mother was dragged to the gallows for the very same dark blood. *Think,* Aya commanded herself, stifling the terror. *Vane is a creature of greed. Give her something bigger than a corpse.* "You leaked the raid yourself," Aya said, dropping the slurred dockside accent she had spent months painstakingly practicing. Her true voice emerged—crisp, refined, and drenched in the arrogant cadence of the High Boroughs. "A fake arrest. A cull to see who would reach for your claim the moment your back was turned." Vane chuckled, a dry, rattling sound. "A sharp mind on a high-born neck. Aye. The Magistrates get a few expendable drunks to show the Governor they’re earning their keep, and I find out which of my lieutenants had the teeth to try for the Scythan iron. I didn't expect *you* to lead them, my sweet. A girl who bends the immateria... and talks like a duchess." Vane raised her pistol, leveling the cold brass double-barrel directly between Aya's eyes. "A witch is bad for business, darling. The Church pays a handsome bounty, but the Inquisitors bring too much light into my dark corners. I think I'll just feed the three of you to the harbor crabs." "Kill me," Aya said, holding her head high, though her breath caught in her throat, "and you burn the greatest leverage you will ever hold in this miserable port." Vane’s thumb lingered on the gun's hammer. "Is that so?" "I am no street-rat playing at high magic, Vane," Aya lied smoothly, weaving half-truths into a lifeline. "I am Lady Aya Vance. Firstborn daughter to the Comptroller of the Admiralty." Simeon let out a breathless, disbelieving curse. Katra stared at her with a mix of horror and profound betrayal. Aya ignored them, keeping her gaze locked onto the guild leader’s yellowed eyes. "My father controls the shipping permits for every leviathan-hunter entering the bay. He signs the tallow tariffs. He commands the privateer escorts. Do you think I joined your guild for pocket copper? I came for the Scythan iron—for power my father denies me because of the blood I inherited." Aya leaned forward against the weight of her iron bindings. "Put a bolt through my head, and you get three bloated bodies in the tide. Keep me alive, and you hold the Admiralty on a leash. My father will pay ten thousand sovereigns in silent draft just to keep my... *indiscretions*... from reaching the High Inquisitor. Or better yet, I can forge you the trade seals that pass your smuggled oil straight through the blockade without a single coin of duty." Silence descended upon the underhold, heavy and suffocating, punctuated only by the rhythmic *drip-drip* of condensation and the steady hiss of the gas lamps. Internal horror warred with Aya's composure. If her father learned of this, she would be locked in the dampest cell of the Iron Order, subjected to nullifying oil and brass screws until her mind unspooled. But to survive the next ten minutes was to live to fight another day. Slowly, agonizingly, Mother Vane lowered the pistol. A slow, terrifying smile spread across her weathered face. "Lady Vance," Vane murmured, tasting the name like rich wine. "Well, now. It seems the haul tonight was far richer than an old Scythan trinket." She motioned lazily to her bodyguards. "Take them to the lower sump. Put them in the heavy iron—the ones forged with cold lead. We wouldn't want our little songbird casting any shadows before we write her dear old papa a letter."
